content_topics: Atoms, elements, molecules and compounds,
Symbols of common elements (oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, iron, aluminium, copper, silver, gold, chlorine, sodium, mercury, lead),
Word equations for reactions of elements to form compounds (sodium chloride, water, carbon dioxide, copper oxide, aluminium oxide),
Uses of some common elements in the society (jewellery, construction, electricity, food nutrients, minerals elements, medals.
learning_experiences: discuss the meaning of atoms, elements, molecules and compounds,
collaboratively sample labelled containers of different substances, identify and record the elements or compounds on the containers,
collaboratively represent selected elements using symbols,
use word equations to represent reactions of elements to form compounds,
identify elements in selected compounds (compounds with only two elements),
explore the importance and value of common elements and compounds in day-to-day life,
use digital or print media to search for information on atoms, elements, molecules and compounds or observe simulations of atoms, elements, molecules and compounds.
key_inquiry_questions: Why is it important to use symbols for representing elements in day-to-day life?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Learning to learn: the learner reflects on their own experiences as they identify elements and compounds on labels of containers.
Communication and Collaboration: the learner writes clearly the symbols of elements, compounds, word equations.
sub_strands.values: Unity: the learner cooperates and harmoniously works with others while identifying elements and compounds from sample-labelled containers of different substances.
sub_strands.pcis: Financial literacy: the learner explores the value of common elements and compounds in society as they learn about importance and value of common elements and compounds in day-to-day life.
sub_strands.links: The learner is able to relate the use of ingredients and items made from the common elements and compounds learnt in Agriculture.

skills.name: Tell an atom, an element, a molecule and a compound apart
skills.mastery: The child says an atom is the smallest particle of an element, an element is made of one kind of atom (oxygen, iron), a molecule is two or more atoms joined (water, oxygen gas) and a compound is made of different elements joined chemically (water, salt). The child does not say a compound is a mixture or an atom is a molecule. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the word from its description
say what a compound is made of
sort substances into elements and compounds
find the false step in a learner's reason

misconceptions.error: Says an atom and a molecule are the same.

example.question: What is a molecule?
example.wrong_answer: The smallest particle of an element
example.correct_answer: Two or more atoms joined together

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes up two ideas that sound alike or are taught close together.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The smallest particle of an element" next to the right answer in a new question and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Build an oxygen molecule from two balls.
misconceptions.feedback: An atom is one particle. A molecule is two or more atoms joined.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says a compound is made of one kind of atom.

example.question: What is a compound?
example.wrong_answer: A substance made of one kind of atom
example.correct_answer: A substance made of different elements joined chemically

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes up two ideas that sound alike or are taught close together.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A substance made of one kind of atom" next to the right answer in a new question and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Compare iron (one kind) and water (hydrogen and oxygen).
misconceptions.feedback: An element has one kind of atom. A compound has different elements joined.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says a compound is the same as a mixture.

example.question: How is a compound different from a mixture?
example.correct_answer: Its elements are joined chemically and cannot be separated easily

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes up two ideas that sound alike or are taught close together.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It is not different" next to the right answer in a new question and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Try to separate iron filings from sand and then iron from iron sulphide.
misconceptions.feedback: The elements in a compound are joined chemically. In a mixture they are only mixed.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gives the first letter of the name for every element (I for iron, S for sodium).

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "I" next to the right answer in a new question and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Some symbols come from old Latin names: ferrum for iron, natrium for sodium.
misconceptions.feedback: Not every symbol is the first letter. Iron is Fe, sodium is Na and potassium is K.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gives the wrong element for a symbol.

misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Puts the product first.

example.question: Which word equation is correct?

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "magnesium oxide gives magnesium + oxygen" next to the right answer in a new question and ask the child to choose.

misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gives the wrong name to the compound (iron sulphate for iron sulphide).

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Iron sulphate" next to the right answer in a new question and ask the child to choose.

misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

content_topics: Kinetic theory of matter,
Heating curve,
Effects of impurities on boiling point and melting point,
Physical and chemical changes (both temporary and permanent changes),
Applications of physical and chemical changes in day-to-day life.
learning_experiences: Carry out activities to demonstrate the characteristics of particles in the three states of matter,
perform experiments to demonstrate diffusion in liquids and gases, for example use of water and ink to illustrate kinetic theory of matter,
carry out experiments to determine the boiling and melting points of pure and impure substances,
draw the heating curve and discuss the trends,
discuss the effects of impurities on boiling point and melting point of a substance,
carry out experiments to demonstrate physical and chemical changes in substances,
discuss the applications of physical and chemical changes in day-to-day life,
use digital or print media to search for the information on movement of particles in the different states of matter.
key_inquiry_questions: How does the movement of particles in matter affect its properties?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Critical thinking and Problem solving: the learner uses logical reasoning during the discussion of the characteristics of particles in the three states of matter.
Digital literacy: the learner gains digital literacy as they use digital media and search for the information on movement of particles in the different states of matter.
sub_strands.values: Unity: the learner cooperates and harmoniously works with peers as they carry out simple experiments to determine the boiling and melting points of pure and impure substances.
sub_strands.pcis: Safety and Security: the learner observes safety to avoid burns while carrying out simple experiments to determine the boiling and melting points of pure and impure substances with peers.
sub_strands.links: The learner relates concept of change of state of matter to preserve food in Agriculture.

skills.name: Describe the particles in solids, liquids and gases
skills.mastery: The child says the particles of a solid are close together in fixed places and only vibrate, the particles of a liquid are close but slide past each other, and the particles of a gas are far apart and move freely in all directions, and does not say solid particles do not move. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

skills.name: Say how impurities change melting and boiling points
skills.mastery: The child says a pure substance melts and boils at fixed temperatures (pure water melts at 0 degrees Celsius and boils at 100), that impurities raise the boiling point and lower the melting point (salty water boils above 100 degrees and freezes below 0), and does not say impurities lower the boiling point. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

skills.name: Tell a physical change from a chemical change
skills.mastery: The child says a physical change makes no new substance and can usually be reversed (melting ice, dissolving sugar, boiling water), a chemical change makes a new substance and is usually not reversible (burning wood, rusting iron, cooking an egg, milk going sour), and does not call burning physical or melting chemical. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: sort a change
say what a new substance shows

content_topics: Causes of fire (classes of fire),
Fire triangle and Fire control (breaking the fire triangle and use of fire extinguishers),
Dangers of fires.
learning_experiences: discuss the possible causes of fire in nature,
discuss the role of the components of fire triangle in the spread of fire,
brainstorm on the different classes of fire,
discuss the dangers of fires in the environment,
collaboratively practice fire control measures,
discuss rights to safety information on flammable substances,

use digital devices or print media to search for information on fire control measures. project: Learner is guided to prepare posters on classes of fires and their control measures and hang them in places where they can be seen.
key_inquiry_questions: What are the dangers of fire in nature?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Citizenship: the learner enhances active community life skills by making posters on classes of fires and their control measures and hanging them at the places where they can be seen.
Communication and Collaboration: the learner acquires listening, speaking, and recording skills as they discuss the causes of fire, dangers of fire and rights to safety
sub_strands.values:
Respect: the learner observes rules of engagement while working with peers to classify fire according to the cause and suggest control measures.
Responsibility: the learner accommodates each other’s views and opinions as they discuss rights to safety information on flammable substances.
sub_strands.pcis: Safety and Security: the learner learns how to take care of self and others when handling fire, as the learner discusses the dangers of fires in the environment.
sub_strands.links: The learner practices safety measures to prevent fire accidents in nature as a life skill in Social Studies.

outcomes.text: identify causes of fire in nature
explain the role of the components of fire triangle in the spread of fire
describe ways of controlling different classes of fires
acknowledge the dangers of fires in nature

skills.name: Say what a fire needs and how taking one away puts it out
skills.mastery: The child says a fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen, that taking away any one puts the fire out (cooling with water removes heat, a blanket removes oxygen, clearing dry grass removes fuel), names natural causes (lightning, volcanic eruptions, dry grass lit by the hot sun) and does not say fire needs only heat and fuel. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: name the parts of the fire triangle
say which part to remove
pick a cause of fire in nature
find the false step in a learner's reason

skills.name: Choose the right way to put out different classes of fire
skills.mastery: The child says water suits a fire of wood, paper or cloth, that an oil or petrol fire is smothered with sand, a blanket or foam and never put out with water, that an electrical fire needs the power switched off and a dry powder or carbon dioxide extinguisher and never water, and that the first step is to raise the alarm and keep safe. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick what puts out a wood fire
pick what to use on an oil fire

content_topics: Cell structure as seen under a light microscope (plant and animal cells),
Preparation of temporary slides of plant cells,
Magnification of cells seen under the light microscope.
learning_experiences: collaboratively prepare, mount, observe and draw plant cells as seen under a light microscope, (include a reminder on how to use and care for a light microscope),

use print and non-print material to search for information on functions of components of plant and animal cells as seen under the light microscope,
discuss the similarities and differences between plant and animal cells as seen under a light microscope,
calculate magnification of specimens at various objective lenses of the light microscope.
key_inquiry_questions: What makes up plant and animal cells?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Learning to learn: the learner learns how to prepare, mount, observe, and draws plant cells as seen under a light microscope.
Self-efficacy: the learner successfully prepares and observes specimens under the light microscope.

skills.name: Name the parts of plant and animal cells and what each does
skills.mastery: The child says both cells have a cell membrane (controls what enters and leaves), cytoplasm (where reactions happen) and a nucleus (controls the cell), and that plant cells also have a cell wall (supports the cell), chloroplasts (make food with light) and a large vacuole (stores sap), and does not give an animal cell a cell wall or a chloroplast. skills.name: Say what diffusion and osmosis are and why living things need them

Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

content_topics: Forms of energy in nature,

sub_strands.values:

Love: the learner cares for self and others as they demonstrate the processes of energy transformation in day-to-day life.
sub_strands.pcis: Safety: the learner learns how to stay safe as they discuss safety measures on energy transformation and mitigation strategies
sub_strands.links: The learner relates the concept of energy transformation to cooking processes in Agriculture.

misconceptions.error: Says pressure in a liquid stays the same with depth.

example.question: How does liquid pressure change with depth?

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes up two ideas that sound alike or are taught close together.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It stays the same" next to the right answer in a new question and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Poke holes at different heights in a bottle.
misconceptions.feedback: Liquid pressure grows with depth, so a dam wall is thicker at the bottom.
